body: @StephenFluin have you looked into the issue at all and could maybe provide your findings? If not, no big deal(: would save me some legwork

Initial findings are that the CLI will first kickof ngcc with `"browser", "module", "main"`, resulting in the ES5 sources being analyzed and because it is the first request, will also update the `.d.ts` files.

That is all fine, however the ES5 analysis ends up completely empty. I found using `ts.Program.getSourceFiles().map(sf => sf.fileName).filter(n => n.endsWith('.js'))` that the program's sources only included the entry point's `index.js`, its import to `./public_api` was not within the list.

So, what is going on? Some more debugging let me to the root problem here: the typing files and JS source files are all located in the same directory. Hence, when TypeScript resolves `./public_api` its module resolution system will end up with `./public_api.d.ts`! Hence, the actually interesting source files that ngcc needs to process never become part of the analysis program; causing ngcc to conclude there's nothing to update in the source nor in the typings but the package is marked as being processed regardless (which is correct).

We'll probably need some way of customizing TypeScript's module resolution system here, such that it prefers '.js' files over '.d.ts'.

cc @m-henderson

@sarunint Thanks for your investigation, it is spot on! If I knew that before it would have saved me a lot of time :) I am actually trying to come up with customized module resolution logic in ngcc to support this.
Well, I spent _hours_ on why ES5 bundle won't compile. Lol

> Well, I spent _hours_ on why ES5 bundle won't compile. Lol

Me too 🤡
Now that the root cause is known, are we going to fix `ivy-ngcc`, or fix AngularFire?
By "fixing AngularFire", I mean "make amendments to Angular Package Format to specify that the bundles (ESM/FESM 5/2015) must be in a subfolder, then make changes to AngularFire".

… imports

Packages that do not follow APF may have the declaration files in the same
directory as one source format, typically ES5. This is problematic for ngcc,
as it needs to create a TypeScript program with all JavaScript sources of
an entry-point, whereas TypeScript's module resolution mechanism would have
resolved an internal module import to the external facing .d.ts declaration
file, instead of the JavaScript source file. This behavior results in the
program to be analysed being incomplete.

This commit introduces a custom compiler host that recognizes the above
scenario and rewires the resolution of a .d.ts declaration file to its
JavaScript counterpart, if applicable.

Fixes #29939
